## Introduction

### Characteristics and discovery of the N400

The N400 is a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) associated with the processing of meaningful stimuli. It typically develops approximately 200–300 ms after stimulus onset and is prominent around 400 ms, although its timing and duration vary with the task and stimulus. For visually presented words, the effect commonly has a broad centroparietal distribution, with substantial activity at central and parietal electrodes. Crucially, the N400 is generally described in terms of amplitude differences between conditions, rather than the presence of a unique negative peak in every waveform [@kutas2011]. In the ERP CORE word-pair paradigm, the representative electrode is CPz and the recommended measurement window is 300–500 ms after target-word onset [@kappenman2021].

The component was first reported by Kutas and Hillyard in 1980. Participants read sentences that ended with either contextually appropriate words or semantically anomalous completions. Unexpected endings elicited a larger negative response around 400 ms, demonstrating that scalp-recorded brain activity was sensitive to linguistic meaning rather than only the physical characteristics of a stimulus [@kutas1980]. This discovery established ERPs as a valuable method for investigating the time course of language comprehension.

### Conditions that elicit the N400

Subsequent research established that N400 amplitude varies systematically with semantic context. Words that are difficult to relate to preceding information tend to elicit larger negative responses than words supported by context. The effect occurs in sentences, isolated word pairs, and other meaningful stimulus sequences; it is not restricted to obvious grammatical or semantic violations [@kutas2011].

In semantic priming experiments, a target such as *butter* following *bread* generally elicits a smaller N400 than the same target following an unrelated prime. Context can facilitate the processing of a word even when both alternatives are meaningful and grammatically acceptable. N400-like effects have also been investigated with pictures, environmental sounds and other conceptually meaningful stimuli, supporting the view that the component is not exclusively a response to written language [@lau2008; @kutas2011].

### Functional significance and theoretical debate

The N400 is widely interpreted as an electrophysiological index of meaning-related processing, but the precise cognitive operation it reflects remains debated. One account emphasises access to or activation of semantic representations: related context preactivates relevant information, reducing the processing required when the target appears. Another emphasises the ease of integrating the target into an evolving representation of context. These interpretations are difficult to distinguish because semantic access, contextual expectations and integration frequently covary in natural language [@lau2008].

More recent frameworks treat N400 amplitude as sensitive to the degree of contextual support for a stimulus, without equating the component with a single, isolated stage of comprehension [@kutas2011].

The present report examines the N400 using the ERP CORE word-pair judgement task. Participants saw related and unrelated prime–target pairs, allowing comparison of target-locked ERPs. Based on previous research, unrelated targets are expected to elicit a more negative-going waveform than related targets at CPz during the 300–500 ms measurement window [@kappenman2021].

## Methods

### Participants

The ERP CORE resource originally included 40 neurotypical young adults from the University of California, Davis community (25 female, 15 male; mean age 21.5 years, SD = 2.87; age range 18–30 years). Thirty-eight participants were right-handed.

Participants reported native English competence, normal colour perception, normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological injury or disease. All provided informed consent.

The original N400 analysis retained 39 participants after task-specific exclusions, including criteria concerning artefact-contaminated trials, response accuracy and the number of trials remaining in each condition [@kappenman2021].

The number of participants included in the present reanalysis will be determined from the available dataset and retained participant averages.

The dataset was made available through the ERP CORE resource under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0) licence.

### Procedure

The N400 was elicited using a semantic word-pair judgement task. Each trial presented a red prime word followed by a green target word. Participants indicated by button press whether the target was semantically related or unrelated to the prime.

The experiment contained 120 trials: 60 related and 60 unrelated, organised into blocks of 20. Each target appeared in both a related and an unrelated context across the experiment.

The prime was displayed for 200 ms, followed by an interstimulus interval of 900–1100 ms. The target was displayed for 200 ms, followed by an intertrial interval of 1400–1600 ms.

The N400 analysis was time-locked to the onset of the target word rather than the prime word [@kappenman2021].

### EEG recording

Continuous EEG was acquired using a BioSemi ActiveTwo system with active electrodes positioned in an elastic cap.

Thirty scalp electrodes were positioned according to the international 10–20 system: Fp1, F3, F7, FC3, C3, C5, P3, P7, P9, PO7, PO3, O1, Oz, Pz, CPz, Fp2, Fz, F4, F8, FC4, FCz, Cz, C4, C6, P4, P8, P10, PO8, PO4 and O2.

The common mode sense (CMS) electrode was positioned at PO1 and the driven right leg (DRL) electrode at PO2.

Horizontal electrooculography (EOG) was recorded using electrodes positioned lateral to both eyes. Vertical EOG was recorded below the right eye and combined with Fp2 offline.

Signals were acquired at a sampling frequency of 1024 Hz with 24-bit resolution. A fifth-order sinc acquisition low-pass filter was applied, with a half-power cutoff of 204.8 Hz.

EEG referencing was performed offline [@kappenman2021].

### Analysis parameters

The present analysis uses the supplied mini_mne preprocessing pipeline. The EEG data are re-referenced to the average of P9 and P10, used as proxies for the mastoid electrodes.

A high-pass filter of 0.1 Hz and low-pass filter of 30 Hz are applied, as permitted by the assessment instructions.

Continuous EEG recordings are segmented into epochs extending from 200 ms before to 800 ms after target-word onset.

Baseline correction is performed using the 200 ms prestimulus interval.

The supplied artefact rejection thresholds are 150 µV for EEG and 250 µV for EOG channels.

ERPs are averaged separately for semantically related and unrelated target words for each participant. Participant averages are subsequently combined to calculate grand-average waveforms for each condition.

The representative electrode for the N400 is CPz, and the analysis window is 300–500 ms after target-word onset [@kappenman2021].

The simplified teaching pipeline does not necessarily reproduce every procedure in the original ERP CORE study, including ICA-based ocular correction, individualised artefact rejection and behavioural exclusions. These differences should be considered when interpreting the results.

#### Preprocessing parameters

```{python}
FILTER_SETTINGS = {
    "low_cutoff": 0.1,
    "high_cutoff": 30.0
}

REFERENCE = ["P9", "P10"]
```

#### Epoching parameters

```{python}
TMIN = -0.2
TMAX = 0.8

BASELINE = (-0.2, 0)

# Check exact event names against your dataset
CONDITIONS = [
    "stimulus/target_word/related",
    "stimulus/target_word/unrelated"
]


REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,
    "eog": 250e-6
}
```

## Data analysis

### Setup

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

from mini_mne import (
    SimpleRaw,
    SimpleEpoch,
    grand_average,
    plot_evokeds
)

from scripts.preproc import preprocess

RAW_PATH = Path("data/raw")
PROCESSED_PATH = Path("data/processed")

PROCESSED_PATH.mkdir(
    parents=True,
    exist_ok=True
)

raw_files = sorted(
    RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz")
)

print(f"Found {len(raw_files)} raw EEG files")

if not raw_files:
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "No EEG files found in data/"
    )

# Check event labels in the first recording
probe = SimpleRaw(raw_files[0])

probe_events, probe_event_id = probe.get_events()

print("Available events:", probe_event_id)

# Check whether N400 condition prefixes exist
missing = [
    cond for cond in CONDITIONS
    if not any(
        label.startswith(cond + "/")
        for label in probe_event_id
    )
]

if missing:
    raise ValueError(
        f"N400 conditions not found: {missing}. "
        "Check the event dictionary and update CONDITIONS."
    )
    print("N400 target conditions found!")
```

### Preprocessing

```{python}
# Find all EEG files
raw_files = sorted(
    RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz")
)

print(f"Found {len(raw_files)} EEG files")

# Preprocess all participants
for raw_file in raw_files:

    print(
        f"Starting: {raw_file.name}",
        flush=True
    )

    # Extract participant ID
    subj_ID = raw_file.name.removesuffix(
        "_raw.fif.gz"
    )

    # Define processed output filename
    output_file = (
        PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz"
    )

    # Skip files that were already processed
    if output_file.exists():
        print(
            f"Already processed: {output_file.name}"
        )
        continue

    # Load raw recording
    raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)

    print(
        "EEG file loaded successfully",
        flush=True
    )

    # Preprocess the EEG recording
    processed = preprocess(
        raw,
        reref_params=REFERENCE,
        filter_low_cutoff=FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"],
        filter_high_cutoff=FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"]
    )

    print(
        "Preprocessing completed",
        flush=True
    )

    # Save processed recording
    processed.save(
        output_file,
        overwrite=True
    )

    print(
        f"Finished: {raw_file.name}",
        flush=True
    )
```

## Epoching and averaging

```{python}
# Define the two N400 conditions
CONDITIONS = [
    "stimulus/target_word/related",
    "stimulus/target_word/unrelated"
]

# Initialise participant average lists
ss_avs = {cond: [] for cond in CONDITIONS}

# Find processed EEG files
processed_files = sorted(
    PROCESSED_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz")
)

print(f"Processed files: {len(processed_files)}")

if not processed_files:
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "No processed EEG files found"
    )

# Define original N400 event labels
related_labels = [
    "stimulus/target_word/related/list1",
    "stimulus/target_word/related/list2"
]

unrelated_labels = [
    "stimulus/target_word/unrelated/list1",
    "stimulus/target_word/unrelated/list2"
]

for processed_file in processed_files:

    print(f"Epoching: {processed_file.name}")

    processed = SimpleRaw(processed_file)

    events, event_id = processed.get_events()

    # Check event labels
    required_labels = related_labels + unrelated_labels

    missing = [
        label for label in required_labels
        if label not in event_id
    ]

    if missing:
        print(
            f"Skipping {processed_file.name}: "
            f"missing {missing}"
        )
        continue

    # Copy events to avoid modifying originals
    combined_events = events.copy()

    related_codes = [
        event_id[label] for label in related_labels
    ]

    unrelated_codes = [
        event_id[label] for label in unrelated_labels
    ]

    # Combine both related lists
    # and both unrelated lists
    for code in related_codes:
        combined_events[
            combined_events[:, 2] == code, 2
        ] = 101

    for code in unrelated_codes:
        combined_events[
            combined_events[:, 2] == code, 2
        ] = 102

    combined_event_id = {
        "stimulus/target_word/related": 101,
        "stimulus/target_word/unrelated": 102
    }

    # Create epochs
    epochs = SimpleEpoch(
        processed,
        combined_events,
        combined_event_id,
        tmin=TMIN,
        tmax=TMAX,
        baseline=BASELINE,
        reject=REJECT
    )

    # Average each condition
    
# Average each condition
participant_averages = {}
participant_valid = True

for cond in CONDITIONS:

    try:
        condition_epochs = epochs[cond]

        print(f"Checking condition: {cond}")

        # Force rejection checks where supported
        n_epochs = len(condition_epochs)

        print(f"Usable epochs: {n_epochs}")

        if n_epochs == 0:
            print(
                f"No usable epochs for {cond} "
                f"in {processed_file.name}"
            )
            participant_valid = False
            break

        av = condition_epochs.average()
        participant_averages[cond] = av

    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(
            f"Epoch averaging failed for "
            f"{processed_file.name}, {cond}: {e}"
        )
        participant_valid = False
        break

# Only include participants with both conditions
if participant_valid:

    for cond in CONDITIONS:
        ss_avs[cond].append(
            participant_averages[cond]
        )

    print(
        f"Participant included: {processed_file.name}"
    )

else:
    print(
        f"Participant excluded: {processed_file.name}"
    )
combined_event_id = {
    "stimulus/target_word/related": 101,
    "stimulus/target_word/unrelated": 102
}

# Count target events before artefact rejection
for cond, code in combined_event_id.items():

    n_events = (
        combined_events[:, 2] == code
    ).sum()

    print(
        f"{processed_file.name} - "
        f"{cond}: {n_events} target events"
    )


# Report number of participant averages
for cond in CONDITIONS:

    print(
        f"{cond}: "
        f"{len(ss_avs[cond])} participant averages"
    )
```

## Grand average

```{python}
# Create grand averages
grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:

    if len(ss_avs[cond]) == 0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"No participant averages for {cond}"
        )

    grand_avs[cond] = grand_average(
        ss_avs[cond]
    )

    print(f"Grand average calculated: {cond}")

print("Grand averaging completed!")
```

## Results

### Grand average N400 effect

```{python}
selected_electrode = "CPz"

analysis_window_start = 0.3
analysis_window_end = 0.5

plot_title = (
    "Grand Average N400: Related versus "
    "Unrelated Word Pairs at CPz"
)

print("Available conditions:", list(grand_avs))

plot_evokeds(
    grand_avs,
    picks=selected_electrode,
    invert_y=True,
    title=plot_title,
    vlines=[
        analysis_window_start,
        analysis_window_end
    ]
)
```

## Results

### Grand average: N400 effect

The grand-average event-related potentials for semantically related and unrelated target words are presented in Figure 1. The analysis focuses on electrode CPz, with the N400 measurement window defined as 300–500 ms after target-word onset.

## Discussion and reflection

The present analysis investigated whether the semantic word-pair task in the ERP CORE dataset elicited the characteristic N400 response. Previous research demonstrates that semantically unrelated targets typically produce a greater negative-going response than related targets, particularly at centroparietal electrode sites during the 300–500 ms post-stimulus interval [@kappenman2021; @kutas2011].

**[Insert your actual findings here.]** Describe whether the unrelated condition demonstrated greater negativity than the related condition at CPz. Discuss the timing and magnitude of the observed difference and whether the overall pattern was consistent with the findings of Kappenman et al. (2021).

If the expected N400 effect was observed, the result would support previous evidence that semantic context facilitates the processing of related target words, resulting in reduced N400 negativity. Such findings are consistent with theories suggesting that the N400 reflects context-sensitive semantic processing [@lau2008].

If the expected effect was reduced or absent, potential explanations include differences in the number of retained participants, artefact rejection, event selection, and preprocessing procedures. The simplified analysis pipeline does not reproduce every stage of the original ERP CORE processing procedure, limiting direct comparisons of waveform amplitudes.

Applying this analysis to a new dataset demonstrated the importance of methodological decisions in ERP research. In particular, I learned that accurate event identification is essential for interpreting stimulus-locked neural responses. Preprocessing choices, including filtering, referencing and artefact rejection, can also influence waveform morphology and the number of usable trials. The process reinforced the importance of documenting analytical decisions to ensure reproducibility and facilitate meaningful comparisons with published findings.
